introduction.text: **Before you start.** In baking you can't taste and adjust as you go: a cake is right or wrong when it comes out of the oven. Three things decide it: the formula (the proportions), the method (how they are combined) and the oven (how it sets them). This course teaches you to read all three:

items.text: **the fundamentals:** baker's percentages, what each ingredient does, tins, ovens and allergens;
**quick breads and batters:** muffins, pancakes and scones;
**shortcrust:** *pâte brisée* and *pâte sucrée*, blind-baked without shrinking;
**cakes:** creamed and foamed, diagnosed from the crumb, and a finished layer cake;
**custards and creams:** *crème pâtissière*, *crème anglaise*, baked custards and whipped cream;
**biscuits:** one variable tested, and a review of your baking log.

introduction.text: *The cross-section is the evidence.* Every bake is cut and photographed: the crumb of a cake, the base and edge of a tart, the rise of a muffin. You band your own result before the AI review and the tasters do, which trains your eye (`JD-REFL`).
*Weigh everything*, including eggs and liquids, on the scale; leaveners and salt on the precision scale.

items.text: **allergens:** every allergen-free bake is made first, with washed tools, and every label is read;

**egg creams:** pastry cream and custards are cooled from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours and to 5 °C within 6 hours, and kept at most 2 days; egg-thickened desserts and Swiss meringue reach 71 °C in every part.

introduction.text: Plan about seven weeks, the longest course of S2. Most bakes fit a weekend afternoon; pastry and custards need time in the fridge. Share the bakes with the household, neighbours or colleagues: they are your tasters.

**Have ready:** the scale and the precision scale; the oven thermometer; the probe; a hand or stand mixer; a 1 kg loaf tin, a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, one or two 20 cm round tins, a muffin tin or paper cases; a rolling pin; a bench scraper; baking paper and baking beans; ramekins; a palette knife; a wire rack; shallow trays and film for cooling; the baking log; the allergen checklist (`SAF-1`); the tasting forms.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BAK-2.M1` in the course file, 2 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a few grams of baking powder, or 10 % more liquid, change a bake visibly, and once it is in the oven nothing can be corrected. Baker's percentages let you see a formula's character at a glance and scale it to any tin.
**You need:** the scale (1 g) and the precision scale (0.1 g); a calculator; the pound-cake and bread formulas of `BAK-2.M1.X1`; the journal.
**Explanation:**

*Why precision.* Everything is weighed: flour, sugar and fat on the scale; leaveners and salt on the precision scale where the quantity is small (`TST-1`). Liquids are weighed too: 1 ml of water weighs 1 g. A cup of flour varies with how it is filled; a weight doesn't.
*Baker's percentages:*

items.text: the total flour is 100 %;
every other ingredient is a percentage of the flour's weight.

blocks.text: A bread of 500 g of flour, 325 g of water, 10 g of salt and 5 g of yeast is 100 %, 65 %, 2 % and 1 %. The percentages show the character of the formula:

items.text: **hydration:** the water as a percentage of the flour (65 % here);
**sweetness:** the sugar;
**richness:** the fat and eggs.

blocks.text: *Scaling:*

items.text: Choose the flour weight, or work it out from the total weight you need: the total divided by the sum of the percentages. For 1 kg of the bread dough above: 1000 ÷ 1.68 = 595 g of flour.
Multiply each percentage by the flour weight: 387 g of water, 12 g of salt, 6 g of yeast.

blocks.text: *Ratios as a memory aid* (`RD-RATO`):

items.text: pound cake 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (flour, butter, sugar, eggs);
shortcrust 2 : 1 (flour to fat);
a basic biscuit 3 : 2 : 1 (flour, fat, sugar).

blocks.text: A ratio card gives you a formula from memory; baker's percentages turn it into grams.
*Eggs in formulas.* A medium egg is about 50 g without its shell: the yolk about 18 g, the white about 32 g. Eggs are weighed, not counted, because sizes vary.
*Tin sizes.* To fit a formula to a different tin, compare the areas of the base: a 23 cm round tin holds about a third more than a 20 cm one (23² ÷ 20² ≈ 1.3).
**Practice:**

items.text: **Convert and scale (45 min).** Write the pound cake and the bread formula in a table with grams and percentages; scale the pound cake from a 20 cm to a 23 cm round tin, and the bread to a 1 kg dough.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a table with grams and percentages for every ingredient; the percentages adding up to the stated total; a scaled formula that fits the tin.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Percentages of the total rather than of the flour
Counting eggs instead of weighing them
Rounding leaveners to the nearest 5 g

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific; the tins and the oven come in `BAK-2.M1.L3`.
**Record:** the two formula tables, with the scaled versions.

**Why it matters:** if you know what each ingredient does, you can predict what a change will do, and read a failed bake backwards to its cause. Without it, a recipe is a set of instructions you can only follow.
**You need:** the muffin formula of `BAK-2.M1.X1`, for the flour comparison; cake flour (*zeeuwse bloem*) and bread flour (*broodmeel*); the journal.
**Explanation:**
*Flour* gives starch for structure, and protein that forms gluten with water and mixing (`SCI-2.M3.L2`).

rows: Bread, rustic bakes; absorbs more water

blocks.text: *Sugar* does more than sweeten:

items.text: it holds water, so a bake stays moist;
it tenderises, because it competes with gluten and starch for water;
it browns (`SC-BRWN`);
in creaming, its crystals trap air.

blocks.text: *Fats:*

items.text: **butter** gives flavour, and its water turns to steam;
**oil** gives a moist, tender crumb;
**solid fat in flakes** gives flaky layers.

blocks.text: Fat coats the flour and shortens the gluten strands: hence "shortcrust".
*Eggs* give structure (the proteins set), emulsify (the yolk), leaven (a whipped foam), and add colour and richness.
*Liquids* hydrate flour and starch, dissolve sugar and salt, and make steam.
*Chemical leaveners:*

items.text: **baking soda** (sodium bicarbonate) needs an acid in the formula, such as buttermilk, yoghurt, honey or brown sugar, and reacts at once;
**baking powder** is soda with its own acid. Most is double-acting: some gas on mixing, more in the oven.

blocks.text: Soda is much stronger than powder, so they are never swapped one for one. Too much leavener gives a coarse crumb, a soapy taste and a collapse.
*Salt* gives flavour; in bread it also controls the yeast and tightens the gluten.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The flour comparison (50 min).** The muffin formula baked twice, once with cake flour and once with bread flour, in the same oven at the same time; cut and photographed in cross-section. This is part of `BAK-2.M1.X1`.

blocks.text: Before you bake, write each ingredient's job in the muffin formula beside its line.
**Look for:** the job of every ingredient written before baking; a visible difference in the crumb, explained.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Bread flour in a tender cake
A soapy, collapsed bake or a flat one
Swapping soda and powder one for one
Use the leavener the formula names
Cutting the sugar in half "for health"
Change sugar in small steps, and expect drier

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the formula annotated with each ingredient's job; the cross-section photos and three sentences on the flour.

**Why it matters:** an oven that runs 20 °C hot, or a tin that sticks, ruins a bake that was weighed perfectly. And flour dust travels: an allergen-free cake can be made unsafe by the bake next to it.

**You need:** a round tin and a loaf tin; baking paper; butter and flour; the oven thermometer; a litre of water and the scale; a 500 g pack of butter; oil and kitchen paper; the cast-iron skillet of `EQP-1`; the calibration log; the allergen checklist.
**Explanation:**
*Preparing tins:*

items.text: grease and line them with baking paper, base and sides for long bakes;
butter and flour fluted tins.

blocks.text: The tin size changes the depth, and so the bake time: a smaller tin means a deeper cake and a longer, lower bake.

*Tin care.* Carbon-steel and tinned tins rust if left wet. Dry them in the cooling oven and keep them lightly oiled. The cast-iron skillet is cared for the same way: seasoned with a thin layer of oil baked on.
*The oven:*

items.text: preheat for at least 15–20 minutes;
check it with the oven thermometer (`EQP-1`), because a dial can be off by 10–20 °C or more;
know its hot spots (`EQP-1.M2`), and turn a tray halfway if one side colours first;
fan ovens bake hotter and faster: set them about 20 °C lower than a conventional oven.

blocks.text: Write the offset on a label on the oven, for example "dial 180 = 165 real".
*Checking the scale.* A litre of water weighs 1000 g, and a 500 g pack of butter about 500 g. Note the results in the calibration log (`KM-EQPT`).
*Allergens in baking* (`SA-ALLG`):

items.text: **the usual ones:** gluten (wheat, spelt, rye, barley, oats), egg, milk, nuts, peanuts, soy, sesame, and lupin (in some flours);
**hidden sources:** chocolate (milk, soy), marzipan (almonds), some baking powders (wheat starch), sprinkles;
**reading labels:** the 14 EU allergen groups are printed in bold (`SAF-1.M4.L1`); "may contain" counts for a severe allergy.

blocks.text: *Cross-contact.* The allergen-free bake is made first, with washed bowls, tins and utensils, and stored apart, covered and labelled. Flour dust settles everywhere: don't sift the ordinary flour while the allergen-free batter stands open.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Tins and oven (40 min).**
Line a round tin and a loaf tin.
Place the oven thermometer, set the dial to 180 °C, and compare after 20 minutes; write the offset on the oven.
Weigh a litre of water.
Oil the carbon-steel tins and season the skillet; photograph them.

blocks.text: **Look for:** tins that release cleanly; the oven offset on a label; no rust.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A pale, sunken or flat bake
Burnt or raw at the stated time
The thermometer and the offset label
Dry in the warm oven; oil lightly
Flour from an ordinary bake dusting an allergen-free one
Allergen-free first, washed tools, stored apart

blocks.text: **Safety:** the allergen rules of `SAF-1.M4`: every label read for the named allergen, "may contain" counted for a severe allergy, the allergen-free bake made first with washed tools and stored apart. Oven gloves for every tin.
**Record:** the calibration log, the offset label, the photos of the tins and skillet.

blocks.text: **Task:** convert three recipes into baker's percentages and scale them; bake the muffins as a flour comparison and as a milk-free batch for a household member or friend; and calibrate your baking equipment.
**You need:** the ingredients below, with both flours; oil and an oat or soy drink; paper cases; the oven thermometer; the allergen checklist; the calibration log.
**Recipe:** the three formulas to convert.

items.text: **Convert** each formula into baker's percentages.
**Scale** the muffins to 12, and the bread to a 1 kg dough (baked in `BRD-2.M2`).
**Calibrate:** log the checks of `BAK-2.M1.L3`, with photos.

**Milk-free batch first:** the scaled muffins with cake flour, 40 g of oil and 10 g of extra plant drink for each 50 g of butter, and plant drink for the milk. Photograph every label. Then wash every bowl and tool.
**The two flour batches:** with cake flour and with bread flour, folded in a dozen strokes (`BAK-2.M2.L1`).
**Bake** all at 200 °C for 5 minutes, then at 180 °C until a skewer comes out clean, about 15–20 minutes.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`KM-MATH` level 3:** the three formulas converted, the muffins scaled and baked; items at 80 %.
**`RD-RATO` level 2, the baking part:** the pound cake from its ratio card; ratio items at 80 %.
**`IN-BAK` level 3:** the flour comparison, explained.
**`SA-ALLG` level 3:** the milk-free batch, labels photographed, checklist ticked; label items at 100 %.
**`KM-EQPT` level 3, the baking part:** the oven and scale checks logged; the skillet and tins photographed.

blocks.text: AI review scores the cross-sections: *competent* is an even, tender crumb in the cake-flour muffin; *not yet* is tunnels, or batches baked at different times.

items.question: A dough has 600 g of flour and 390 g of water. What is its hydration in baker's percentage?
A formula is flour 100 %, water 70 %, salt 2 %, yeast 1 %. How much of each for 800 g of flour?
items.answer: Water 560 g, salt 16 g, yeast 8 g.
items.why: Multiply each percentage by the flour weight.

items.question: You need 1 kg of the dough in Q2 (total 173 %). How much flour?
items.why: Total weight divided by the sum of the percentages.

items.question: A pound cake is 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 by weight. You have 3 eggs of about 50 g each without the shell. How much flour, butter and sugar?
Which flour suits a tender sponge cake?
items.why: Less protein, less gluten, a tender crumb.

items.question: A muffin formula with buttermilk uses baking soda. Why does it work without baking powder?

options.text: the acid in buttermilk reacts with the soda to release gas

items.why: Soda needs an acid in the formula.

items.question: You bake a milk-free cake for an allergic friend alongside a normal one. What is right?

options.text: the milk-free cake first, with washed tools and tins, stored apart, and every label checked
it doesn't matter if they bake separately

items.question: Which baking ingredient can hide milk?
items.why: Many chocolates contain milk or traces; read the label.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BAK-2.M2` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the muffin method is the quickest bake there is: two bowls and a dozen strokes. Its one rule, mix as little as possible, is the first lesson in controlling gluten, and it carries into pancakes, quick breads and cakes.

**You need:** the muffin formula scaled to 12 (`BAK-2.M1.X1`), twice; 240 g of buttermilk and 4 g of baking soda for the soda batch; two bowls; a whisk and a spatula; paper cases; the oven thermometer; a skewer; a timer.
**Explanation:**
*The method:*

items.text: Whisk the dry ingredients together: flour, leavener, salt, and the sugar.
Whisk the wet ones together: eggs, milk or buttermilk, melted butter or oil.
Pour the wet into the dry.
Fold with a spatula in about a dozen strokes, until just combined. A few streaks and lumps remain.

blocks.text: *Why minimal mixing.* Mixing develops gluten. A beaten muffin batter bakes tough, with a peaked top and long tunnels running up through the crumb.
*Soda versus powder:*

items.text: **soda** reacts at once with the acid (here, the buttermilk), so the batter goes into the oven without delay;
**double-acting powder** gives a second rise in the oven, so the batter can wait a little.

blocks.text: A formula with an acid ingredient and too little soda bakes dense and tastes sour; too much soda tastes soapy and browns too fast.

*Baking.* A hot start, about 200 °C, sets the edges and pushes the centre up into a dome; then lower, to 180 °C, to bake through. Fill the cases about three-quarters full. Done when a skewer in the centre comes out clean and the top springs back.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Mixed right and mixed wrong (45 min).** Two batches of the same formula: one folded in a dozen strokes, one beaten for a minute with the whisk. Bake them on the same tray, cut and photograph them.

**Soda and powder (45 min).** One batch with milk and baking powder; one with 240 g of buttermilk for the milk and 4 g of baking soda instead of the powder. Compare the rise, the colour and the taste.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a lumpy batter that is barely mixed; muffins with rounded tops and an even, tender crumb, without tunnels.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Batter left standing too long with soda
An oven not up to heat

blocks.text: **Safety:** a hot tray and the oven door: gloves on both hands.
**Record:** the four cross-section photos and a line on each.
**Why it matters:** a stack of *pannenkoeken* is a Dutch dinner, and a batch of scones is ready in half an hour. Both are about judging a batter or dough by eye and hand, rather than by the clock.

**You need:** for thick pancakes, 200 g of flour, 10 g of baking powder, 25 g of sugar, a pinch of salt, an egg, 250 ml of milk, 30 g of melted butter; for *pannenkoeken*, 250 g of flour, 2 eggs, 500 ml of milk, a pinch of salt; toppings (leek and cheese, or bacon and *stroop*); for scones, the formula of `BAK-2.M2.X1`; a frying pan; a cutter.
**Explanation:**
*Pancakes:*

items.text: **thick pancakes:** the muffin method, with a thicker batter that is rested briefly;

**Dutch *pannenkoeken*** and *crêpes*: a thin batter whisked smooth and rested for 30 minutes, so the gluten relaxes and the starch hydrates. Whisk the eggs and half the milk into the flour first, to a smooth paste, then the rest.

blocks.text: Cook them in a medium-hot pan, lightly greased. The first one tests the heat: too pale and greasy means the pan is too cold, and dark spots before the top sets mean it is too hot. Turn thick pancakes when bubbles burst on the surface and stay open.
*Rubbing in (scones):*

items.text: Cut cold butter into the flour and rub it with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs. The fat coats the flour and stays in small pieces, which make steam and flakiness.
Add the liquid and bring it together with a knife.
Pat it out about 2.5 cm thick, without kneading.
Cut straight down, without twisting, so the scones rise evenly.

blocks.text: *Judging the dough and batter:*

items.text: a scone dough is soft and slightly sticky, not dry;
a pancake batter coats a spoon and flows.

blocks.text: Each is adjusted with a spoon of flour or liquid, not by kneading or more whisking.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Pancakes (45 min).** A thick pancake batter and a thin *pannenkoek* batter; a stack of each for breakfast or dinner, with seasonal toppings: leek and cheese, or bacon and *stroop*.
**Scones (45 min).** Rubbed-in scones, cut and baked in a hot oven (about 200 °C); one scone twisted as it is cut, to see the uneven rise.

blocks.text: **Look for:** an even golden colour on the pancakes, with bubbles that burst before turning; tall scones with straight sides and a split middle.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Heat it; test with the first one
Butter rubbed in until it melts
Cold butter, cool fingertips, work quickly
Pat it out; bring it together only

blocks.text: **Safety:** hot fat in the pan; a dry pan handle turned away from the edge. Pancakes with bacon are cooked until the bacon is crisp.
**Record:** photos of the stacks and of the scones, including the twisted one.

**Task:** make muffins and scones from the course formulas, weighed, to standard: an even rise and a tender crumb. Choose a flavouring, savoury or seasonal: cheese and spring onion, pumpkin, carrot, or rhubarb in spring. Band each bake on the form before the AI review.

**You need:** for 12 muffins and 8 scones: 600 g of flour; butter; eggs; milk or buttermilk; baking powder and soda; sugar; salt; the flavouring; paper cases; a 6 cm cutter; the scale; the oven thermometer.
**Recipe:**

*Muffins (12):* 300 g of flour, 150 g of sugar, 10 g of baking powder, 3 g of salt, 2 eggs (100 g), 240 g of milk, 100 g of melted butter, and 150 g of grated carrot or pumpkin, or diced rhubarb. For savoury muffins: 20 g of sugar, 100 g of grated cheese and 3 spring onions.
*Scones (8):* 300 g of flour, 15 g of baking powder, 3 g of salt, 30 g of sugar (none for savoury), 75 g of cold butter in cubes, 1 egg beaten with milk to 175 g.

items.text: **Weigh** everything; leaveners and salt on the precision scale. Check the oven with the thermometer.

**Muffins:** whisk the dry, whisk the wet, toss the flavouring through the dry, then fold in a dozen strokes. Fill the cases three-quarters. Bake at 200 °C for 5 minutes, then 180 °C until a skewer comes out clean, about 15–20 minutes.

**Scones:** rub the butter into the dry ingredients to breadcrumbs. Keep a spoon of the egg mixture for brushing, and bring the rest in with a knife. Pat out 2.5 cm thick, and cut straight down. Brush the tops, and bake at about 200 °C until risen and golden, about 12–15 minutes.
**Cool** on a rack. Cut one of each through the middle.
**Photograph** the cross-sections and the tops.
**Band** them yourself on the form.

blocks.text: **Show:** **`TS-BAK` level 3, the quick-bread element:** muffins and scones from weighed formulas, with an even rise and a tender crumb, without tunnels.

AI review scores the cross-sections against the reference images: *competent* is a rounded muffin with an even, tender crumb, and a tall, straight-sided scone with flaky layers; *not yet* is a peaked muffin with tunnels, or a squat, dense scone. The rubric: even rise, no tunnels, tender crumb (each yes or no).

items.question: Why are muffins tough, peaked and full of tunnels?
What does baking soda need to work?

options.text: an acid in the formula, such as buttermilk or yoghurt

items.question: A batter with baking soda waits for an hour before baking. What happens?

options.text: much of the gas escapes, so the muffins bake flat and dense

items.question: What does double-acting baking powder do?

options.text: releases some gas on mixing and more in the oven

items.question: Muffins taste soapy and are very brown. The likely cause?
items.why: Excess soda tastes soapy and speeds browning.

items.question: Your scone dough is dry and crumbly and won't come together. What do you do?
items.answer: Add liquid a spoonful at a time and bring it together with a knife, without kneading; a scone dough should be soft and slightly sticky.
items.why: Adjust by liquid, not by working.

items.question: Why is a *pannenkoek* batter rested for 30 minutes?

options.text: so the gluten relaxes and the starch hydrates, for tender, even pancakes

items.question: Why is the scone cutter pressed straight down without twisting?

options.text: twisting seals the edges, so the scone rises unevenly

items.why: Open edges let it rise straight.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a short, crisp pastry base is what makes a quiche or a tart. It is three ingredients and a few minutes' work; what goes wrong is almost always warm butter, too much water or no rest.
**You need:** 200 g of plain flour; 100 g of cold butter in cubes; 2 g of salt; about 40–50 g of iced water; an egg yolk (optional); a bowl; a knife or fork; film; the scale.
**Explanation:**

*The formula:* about 2 : 1 flour to cold butter by weight, a pinch of salt, and just enough cold water, about 20–25 % of the flour (40–50 g for 200 g), to bring it together. An egg yolk, in place of some of the water, adds richness and makes it easier to handle.
*Rubbing in:*

items.text: cut the cold butter into the flour with your fingertips, a pastry cutter or a few pulses of a food processor;
stop when it looks like coarse crumbs with some pea-sized pieces of butter left;
work quickly, and lift the crumbs as you rub, so your hands don't warm the butter.

blocks.text: *Water, sparingly.* Add it a spoon at a time and mix with a knife or fork until the dough just holds when you squeeze a handful. More water develops more gluten, and the pastry turns tough and shrinks in the oven. Note the water you used: flours vary, and next time you'll know.

*Gluten and fat.* Fat coats the flour and shortens the gluten strands. The more evenly the butter is rubbed in, the more tender and short the pastry; the bigger the pieces, the flakier, because they melt into steam pockets.

*Resting.* Press the dough into a flat disc, wrap it and chill it for at least an hour. The gluten relaxes and the butter firms, so the pastry rolls easily and shrinks less. Wrapped well, it keeps in the freezer for later use: thaw it in the fridge.
**Practice:**

items.text: ***Pâte brisée* (45 min, plus an hour's rest).** One batch rubbed in by hand; the water used noted; rested, then kept or frozen for `BAK-2.M3.L2`.

blocks.text: **Look for:** coarse crumbs with visible butter; a dough that just holds together; no greasy, sticky patches.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Fingertips only; chill the bowl if needed
A spoon at a time; squeeze-test
Pastry that springs back and tears
At least an hour in the fridge

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific; a food processor blade is lifted out before you scrape the bowl.
**Record:** the water used and a photo of the crumbs and the disc.
**Why it matters:** a tart lives or dies by its base. Shrunken sides spill the filling, and a soggy base makes the whole slice limp. Both are prevented before the filling goes in.

**You need:** the *brisée* of `BAK-2.M3.L1`, and a second batch; two 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tins (or one, used twice); a rolling pin; flour for dusting; baking paper; baking beans, dried beans or rice; an egg for the wash; a sheet pan; the oven thermometer.
**Explanation:**
*Rolling:*

items.text: on a lightly floured surface, from the centre outwards;
turn the dough a quarter after every few rolls, so it stays round and doesn't stick;
to an even 3–4 mm, and a circle about 5 cm wider than the tin.

blocks.text: *Lining:*

items.text: Roll the pastry over the pin and drape it over the tin.
Ease it into the corners without stretching it: lift the edge and let it drop in. Stretched pastry shrinks back.
Leave a little overhang.
Chill the lined tin for 20–30 minutes.

blocks.text: *Blind baking:*

items.text: Preheat the oven with a sheet pan on the shelf.
Line the pastry with crumpled baking paper and fill it to the top with baking beans, dried beans or rice.
Bake on the hot pan at about 180–190 °C until the edges are set and pale gold.
Lift out the paper and beans, and bake again until the base is dry and golden.
Trim the overhang with a sharp knife after baking, for a clean edge.

blocks.text: *Preventing shrinking and soggy bases:*

items.text: **against shrinking:** a rested, unstretched dough, chilled in the tin, and the beans filled to the top so the sides are supported until they set;
**against a soggy base:** a fully blind-baked base, brushed with egg wash in the last minutes to seal it, a hot oven shelf or pan, and the filling added just before baking.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Line and blind bake (60 min).** Roll and line a 23 cm tin; chill; blind bake fully; photograph the base and edge.
**Fix a fault (45 min).** Line a second tin, stretching the pastry and skipping the chill on purpose; blind bake; photograph and compare the shrinking.

blocks.text: **Look for:** an even thickness; the edges standing up straight after baking; a dry, golden base without cracks.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Stretching the pastry into the tin
Ease it in; lift and drop
Rolling unevenly, so it bakes unevenly
Removing the beans too early, so the sides slump
Edges set and pale gold first
Bake on until dry and golden; egg wash

blocks.text: **Safety:** baking beans hold heat for a long time: lift them out in the paper, with gloves, into a heatproof bowl.
**Record:** the photos of both shells side by side.

**Why it matters:** a sweet tart needs a sweet, crisp shell that tastes like a fine biscuit. *Pâte sucrée* is made the other way round from *brisée*: the butter is creamed, not rubbed in, and the dough is soft, so it needs different handling.

**You need:** 200 g of plain flour; 100 g of soft butter; 70 g of icing sugar; 1 egg (about 50 g); a pinch of salt; a bowl and a spatula or the mixer; two sheets of baking paper; a rolling pin; a 23 cm tart tin; film.
**Explanation:**
*Pâte sucrée* is a sweet, crisp, biscuit-like pastry, made by the creaming method:

items.text: Cream the soft butter with the icing sugar and salt until smooth.
Beat in the egg.
Mix in the flour just until combined. Stop as soon as no dry flour shows.

blocks.text: The sugar and the creaming give a fine, crisp crumb. Overmixing after the flour develops gluten and makes it tough and prone to shrinking.
*A soft dough:*

items.text: press it into a flat disc, wrap it and chill it well, at least an hour;
roll it between two sheets of baking paper, so it doesn't stick or need extra flour;
if it softens while you work, slide it, still in the paper, onto a tray and chill it for 10 minutes;
patch any cracks with off-cuts, pressed in: *sucrée* forgives patching, unlike *brisée*.

blocks.text: *Lining and baking.* Line the tin as for *brisée*, and chill it. Bake at a slightly lower heat than *brisée*, about 170–180 °C, because the sugar browns quickly. Blind bake it the same way, with paper and beans, then without, until the shell is an even golden brown.
*Uses:* fruit tarts, the cream tart of `BAK-2.M3.X2`, and small tartlets. A lined, unbaked shell freezes well, and can go into the oven from frozen.

items.text: ***Pâte sucrée* (45 min, plus an hour's rest).** Creamed, chilled, rolled between paper, lined, and frozen for `BAK-2.M3.X2`.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a smooth, soft dough that firms in the fridge; rolled without tearing between the papers; a lined shell with even sides.

rows: Stop when no dry flour shows
A burnt edge, a pale base
Baking too hot, so the edge burns

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.

options.text: so it stays in pieces coating the flour, and doesn't melt into the dough

items.question: Your pastry is tough and shrinks badly. Most likely cause?

options.text: too much water and working, which developed gluten

options.text: the gluten relaxes and the butter firms, so it rolls easily and shrinks less

items.question: Your blind-baked tart shell shrank down the sides of the tin. Name two causes and two fixes.
items.answer: Stretched while lining, or not rested or chilled; ease the pastry in without stretching, rest the dough and chill the lined tin before baking (and leave an overhang to trim after).

all-in-one in a food processor only

items.why: The creaming method gives a fine, crisp crumb.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `BAK-2.M4` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** most home cakes, from a Dutch *cake* to a Victoria sponge, are made by creaming. The rise starts in the bowl, as air beaten into butter and sugar; if it isn't there before the oven, no baking powder fully makes up for it.

**You need:** for the pound cake: 200 g each of butter, sugar, eggs and flour, 4 g of baking powder, a pinch of salt; two small loaf tins for the creaming test; for the sponge: the same formula again, in two 20 cm round tins; the mixer; a spatula; a skewer; a rack.
**Explanation:**
*Creaming:*

items.text: Beat soft butter (cool to the touch, about 18–20 °C) with the sugar for 3–5 minutes, until pale and fluffy. The sugar crystals cut air pockets into the fat, and that air is the start of the rise.

Add the eggs at room temperature, one at a time or in a thin stream, beating well after each. The yolk's emulsifiers hold the water of the egg in the fat. Cold eggs, or eggs added too fast, split the mixture, which looks curdled. A spoon of the flour rescues it.
Fold in the flour (sifted with the baking powder and salt), and any liquid, gently, just until combined, so the air stays in and little gluten develops.

blocks.text: *Butter cakes* made this way: pound cake (*cake* in Dutch), *boterkoek*-style cakes, a Victoria sponge. The baking powder supports the creamed air; it doesn't replace it.

*Baking.* Bake in the middle of the oven at about 170–180 °C, and don't open the door until the cake has set, at least two-thirds of the way through: a draught of cold air can make a rising cake sink.

*Done* when a skewer in the centre comes out clean, the top springs back when pressed lightly, and the cake shrinks just away from the tin. Cool it in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn it out onto a rack.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A pound cake, two creaming times (60 min, plus baking).** One batch of batter, split: half creamed for 1 minute, half for 5 minutes (cream the butter and sugar in two bowls), in two small loaf tins. Bake side by side, cut and photograph.
**A Victoria-style sponge (60 min, plus baking).** Creamed, in two 20 cm tins, for the layer cake of `BAK-2.M4.L4`. Cool, wrap and freeze or keep them for a day.

blocks.text: **Look for:** butter and sugar pale and fluffy; a smooth, uncurdled mixture after the eggs; a flat or gently domed top with an even crumb.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Butter cool to the touch, about 18–20 °C
A curdled mixture, a dense cake
Room-temperature eggs; a spoon of flour

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific beyond the hot tins: gloves, and the rack ready before the cake comes out.
**Record:** the creaming-test photo, the oven reading and the bake times in the baking log.

**Why it matters:** a *génoise* has no baking powder at all: it rises on the air in an egg foam. Learning to whisk to the ribbon and fold without losing that air is the skill behind sponges, rolled cakes and many desserts.

**You need:** 4 eggs, 125 g of sugar, 125 g of flour, 30 g of butter; a heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water; the mixer; a large spatula; a sieve; a lined 20 cm tin; a second set of eggs and sugar for the whisking test.
**Explanation:**
*A foam does the rising:*

items.text: Whisk whole eggs and sugar over a bain-marie until just warm to the touch, about body temperature, then off the heat, until they triple in volume and reach the ribbon stage (`SAU-2.M5.L1`): batter falling from the whisk lies on the surface for a few seconds before sinking.
Sift and fold in the flour, in two or three parts.
Fold in the melted, cooled butter.

blocks.text: The air in the egg foam expands in the oven, and the egg proteins set around it.

*Foams* (`SC-EMUL`). A foam is gas dispersed in a liquid, stabilised by proteins. Sugar stabilises an egg foam; fat and rough folding collapse it. Warming helps the sugar dissolve and the eggs whisk higher.
*Folding:*

items.text: use a large spatula: cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom and turn the batter over, while turning the bowl;
add the flour in two or three parts, sifted over the surface;
mix the melted butter first with a spoonful of batter, then fold that in, so the heavy fat doesn't sink and knock out the air.

blocks.text: *Baking.* Straight into the lined tin and into the oven at once, at about 180 °C, because the foam starts to collapse as it waits. Done when it springs back when pressed and shrinks from the sides.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Whisk to the ribbon (60 min).** Two bowls of 2 eggs and 60 g of sugar: one warmed over the bain-marie, one cold. Whisk each for the same time; photograph the volume and the ribbon. Use both foams in an omelette or a batch of biscuits rather than throwing them away.
**A *génoise* (60 min, plus baking).** Folded, baked, cooled, cut through and photographed.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a pale, thick foam that holds a ribbon for a few seconds; a batter that stays light after folding; an even, fine, springy crumb.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Whisk to a ribbon that holds
Flour pockets or a heavy batter
A greasy, dense layer at the base
Butter poured in hot or all at once

blocks.text: **Safety:** steam from the bain-marie scalds: an oven glove on the hand that holds the bowl.
**Record:** the ribbon photos, the cross-section and the log entry.

**Why it matters:** a cake that went wrong tells you why, if you cut it and read the crumb. Diagnosing from evidence, and changing one thing next time, is how a baker improves, rather than blaming the oven or the recipe.
**You need:** the course's five photos of faulty cakes; your own bakes from `BAK-2.M4.L1` and `BAK-2.M4.L2` and their log entries; the baking log.
**Explanation:**
*Reading the crumb:*

rows: Too much leavener or sugar; oven door opened early; underbaked
Weigh the leavener; check the oven; bake to the skewer
Oven too hot; too much flour; too much mixing
Lower the heat (check with the thermometer); weigh the flour; fold less
Under-creamed; a collapsed foam; too little leavener; curdled batter
Overbaked; too little fat or sugar; too much flour

blocks.text: *Cut it to look.* Cut through the centre with a serrated knife, top to bottom, and photograph the face in good light. Look at the top (flat, domed, cracked, sunken), the crumb (even, coarse, tunnelled, dense), the base (a dense wet streak?) and the edges.

*One fault, one change.* The cause is diagnosed from the crumb and the log: the time, the oven reading and the weights. A dense cake from a log that shows cold eggs points at the eggs, not the oven. The next bake changes one thing, so its effect can be seen. Change three things and you won't know which one worked.
*The baking log* records every bake: the formula, the weights, the oven reading, the time, a photo, your band, and the AI or taster band. It is the evidence for `BAK-2.M6.L2`.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Diagnose five crumbs (40 min).** The course's five photos of faulty cakes, plus your own bakes so far: name the most likely cause and the one change for each, in the log.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a diagnosis that names the most likely cause from evidence, and a single change.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Blaming the oven without checking it
A diagnosis from the top alone
Not cutting the cake to look

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the five diagnoses in the log.

lessons.title: Buttercreams, fillings and finishing a cake

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a birthday cake is the bake people remember. Filling and finishing it neatly takes patience and cold, not talent; and a buttercream that splits can nearly always be rescued.

**You need:** the two sponges of `BAK-2.M4.L1`; for the buttercream, the formula of `BAK-2.M4.X3`; a bain-marie; the probe; the mixer; a serrated knife; a palette knife; a cake board or plate; a compote (optional).
**Explanation:**
*American buttercream:* soft butter beaten with icing sugar and a little milk. It is quick, sweet and stable.
*Swiss meringue buttercream:*

items.text: Whisk egg whites and sugar over a bain-marie until the sugar has dissolved and every part reaches at least 71 °C on the probe (the egg-thickened row of assessment §9, which names Swiss meringue).
Whip it to a stiff, glossy meringue, and keep whipping until it has cooled to room temperature.
Beat in soft butter piece by piece. It may look curdled halfway: keep beating.

blocks.text: It is less sweet and silky.
*Why it splits, and the rescue.* Buttercream is an emulsion of fat and the water in the meringue.

items.text: **Too cold** (the butter or the meringue): it curdles and looks lumpy. Warm the bowl briefly over the bain-marie or with a warm towel, and beat.
**Too warm:** it turns soupy. Chill it for 15 minutes, and beat again.

blocks.text: Never throw a split buttercream away: one of these two fixes nearly always works.
*Finishing a layer cake:*

items.text: Level the cooled cakes with a serrated knife, and split them if needed.
Fill them: buttercream, a compote, or a cream.
Apply a thin crumb coat, which seals in the crumbs, and chill it until firm.
Apply a final coat, smoothed with the palette knife while you turn the plate.

blocks.text: Chilling between steps makes each easier. A finished buttercream cake is kept in the fridge, and taken out a while before serving so the buttercream softens.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Buttercream and a cake (75 min, over two days).** A Swiss meringue buttercream, deliberately split by adding butter that is too cold, then rescued; the sponges of `BAK-2.M4.L1` filled, crumb-coated, chilled overnight and finished.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a silky buttercream that holds a peak; a level cake with straight sides; no crumbs in the final coat.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Warm it or chill it, and beat

blocks.text: **Safety:** the Swiss meringue reaches 71 °C in every part, probed (assessment §9). The finished cake is kept in the fridge and eaten within 2 days.
**Record:** photos of the split and the rescue, and the finished cake.

**Task:** make a creamed butter cake and a foamed *génoise* from weighed formulas, with the intended crumb in each. Before baking, write the textures: the butter cake tender, fine and moist; the *génoise* light, springy and open-fine. Cut each cake through the middle, photograph the cross-section and band it yourself.

**You need:** for the pound cake: 200 g each of butter, sugar, eggs and flour, 4 g of baking powder, a pinch of salt, a lined 1 kg loaf tin; for the *génoise*: 4 eggs, 125 g of sugar, 125 g of flour, 30 g of butter, a lined 20 cm tin; the mixer; a bain-marie; the oven thermometer; a skewer; the tasting forms.
**Recipe:**

items.text: **Name** the textures in writing. Weigh everything; take the butter and eggs out of the fridge an hour ahead.

**Pound cake:** cream the butter and sugar for 5 minutes; beat in the eggs a little at a time; fold in the flour sifted with the baking powder and salt. Bake at about 170 °C. Start testing with a skewer at 45 minutes; it usually needs about an hour. Log the oven reading and the time.

***Génoise:*** melt the butter and let it cool. Whisk the eggs and sugar over the bain-marie until just warm, then off the heat to the ribbon; photograph the ribbon. Fold in the flour in three parts, then the butter loosened with a spoon of batter. Bake at once, at about 180 °C, until it springs back, about 25–30 minutes.
**Cool** both: 10 minutes in the tin, then on the rack.
**Cut** each through the middle and photograph the cross-sections.
**Band** them yourself; then share them with the household or neighbours, who fill in the forms.
**Write** two sentences each on the foam of the *génoise* and the emulsion of the creamed batter.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-BAK` level 3, the cake element:** a cake with an even crumb from a weighed formula.
**`FL-TEXT` level 2:** the intended textures named and hit, with the cross-sections and the tasters' forms.
**`SC-EMUL` level 3:** an egg foam at the ribbon held through folding, and the creamed emulsion, explained; this check at 80 %.

blocks.text: AI review scores the crumb photos against the reference images: *competent* is an even, fine crumb with a flat or gently domed top; *not yet* is a sunken centre, tunnels, or a dense, wet layer at the base. The rubric: even crumb, level top, no dense layer (each yes or no).

exercises.description: A two-layer cake, filled and finished with buttercream; photo of the cut slice.

blocks.text: **Task:** fill and finish a two-layer cake with Swiss meringue buttercream for an occasion (a birthday or a visit), rescue the buttercream if it splits, and photograph the cut slice. If the buttercream doesn't split, split a small portion on purpose by chilling it, and rescue that.

**You need:** two sponges from `BAK-2.M4.L1`, or a *génoise* split in two; 4 egg whites (about 130 g); 200 g of sugar; 300 g of soft butter in cubes; vanilla; a compote (rhubarb in spring, or another seasonal fruit); the bain-marie; the probe; the mixer; a serrated knife; a palette knife.
**Recipe:**

items.text: **Compote (the day before):** 300 g of rhubarb in pieces with 60 g of sugar, simmered until soft, about 10 minutes; cooled and chilled.
**Meringue:** whisk the whites and sugar in a clean bowl over the bain-marie until the sugar has dissolved and every part reaches at least 71 °C on the probe (assessment §9). Log the reading.

**Butter:** beat in the soft butter a cube at a time, then the vanilla. If it curdles, warm the bowl briefly and beat; if it turns soupy, chill it for 15 minutes and beat. Photograph the split and the rescue.
**Level** the sponges with the serrated knife. Fill with a ring of buttercream at the edge, the compote inside it, and the second sponge on top.

**`SC-EMUL` level 3:** a buttercream emulsion split and rescued, photographed before and after, with the cause explained.

items.question: What makes a *génoise* rise?

options.text: the air whisked into the eggs, which expands in the oven and is set by the egg proteins

items.question: Why are eggs and sugar warmed before whisking for a *génoise*?

options.text: the sugar dissolves and the eggs whisk to a higher, more stable foam

items.question: What collapses an egg foam?
items.why: Fat breaks the protein films around the bubbles.

items.question: A Swiss meringue buttercream looks curdled and lumpy. What is wrong, and what do you do?

items.why: A cold buttercream curdles; gentle warmth brings it back.

items.question: A cake has sunk in the centre and is sticky inside. Name the likely causes and your next change.

items.why: The edges set before the middle rises.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** pastry cream fills tarts, choux and cakes. Its rule is the opposite of a *crème anglaise*: it must boil. Knowing why each does what it does is the key to both, and to keeping them safely.

**You need:** for the pastry cream, the quantities of `BAK-2.M5.X1`; for the *crème anglaise*, 250 ml of milk, 3 yolks, 40 g of sugar, vanilla; a heavy pan; a whisk; a sieve; the probe; a shallow tray and film; a bowl in an ice bath.
**Explanation:**
*Crème pâtissière* (pastry cream): milk, yolks, sugar and a starch (cornflour or flour), boiled to a thick, smooth cream.
*The method:*

items.text: Heat the milk with the vanilla.
Whisk the yolks, sugar and starch together.
Temper them: whisk in a third of the hot milk.
Return everything to the pan, and whisk constantly, into the corners, as it comes to the boil.
Boil for 1–2 minutes, still whisking.

blocks.text: *Why it must boil.* The starch must gelatinise fully to thicken and lose its raw taste. The boil also destroys an enzyme in the yolk (amylase) that would otherwise digest the starch and thin the cream overnight. The starch protects the yolk from curdling, so boiling is safe here.

*Why a crème anglaise mustn't boil.* With no starch, the yolks set and curdle above about 84 °C. It is stirred over gentle heat to *nappe*, about 80–84 °C on the probe (`EGG-1.M4.L1`), when it coats the spoon and a finger drawn through it leaves a clean line. Then it is strained at once into a cold bowl.
*Cooling safely* (assessment §9):

items.text: Spread the pastry cream in a shallow tray.
Cover the surface with film, against a skin.
Cool it from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, and to 5 °C within 6 hours in total, probing and logging the times.
Keep it covered in the fridge, at most 2 days.

blocks.text: The *crème anglaise* is cooled the same way, stirred in its bowl over the ice bath.
**Practice:**

items.text: ***Crème pâtissière* (45 min).** Boiled for the full time; cooled in a tray with the temperature logged.
***Crème anglaise* (40 min).** Stirred to *nappe*, the temperature probed, strained and cooled in an ice bath; served with a baked fruit or the cake of `BAK-2.M4`.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a pastry cream thick, glossy and smooth after the boil; a *crème anglaise* that coats the spoon with a clean line through it, without grains.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A cream that is runny next day
Pastry cream taken off before it boils, so it thins overnight
Lumps from not whisking into the corners
A *crème anglaise* boiled until it curdles
A deep bowl of hot cream in the fridge
A shallow tray; the ice bath

blocks.text: **Safety:** the cooling rule of assessment §9: from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours and to 5 °C within 6 hours, then at most 2 days in the fridge. Hot pastry cream spits as it boils: a long whisk, and a sleeve over your wrist.
**Record:** the cooling log for both creams.

**Why it matters:** a *crème caramel* is eggs, milk and sugar, set in the oven. Silky or grainy depends on gentle heat and on knowing when to take it out, which you judge by a wobble rather than a timer.
**You need:** for four ramekins and one larger dish: 150 g of sugar for the caramel; 500 ml of milk; 3 eggs and 2 yolks; 60 g of sugar; vanilla; a deep roasting tin; a kettle; the probe; a timer.
**Explanation:**
*A baked custard:* eggs, milk or cream and sugar, set in the oven without starch. Examples are *crème caramel*, *crème brûlée* and *pots de crème*.

*The water bath.* The ramekins stand in a deep tin of hot water, which comes halfway up their sides, in a moderate oven (about 150–160 °C). The water never goes above 100 °C, so the custard sets gently and evenly, without bubbles or curdling. Pour the hot water in with the tin already on the oven shelf, so you don't carry it full.
*Crème caramel:*

items.text: Make a caramel: sugar heated dry, or with a little water, until deep amber (`SAU-2`). Pour it at once into the moulds and tilt to coat the bases.
Warm the milk with the vanilla; whisk it gently into the eggs, yolks and sugar without making foam; strain it.
Pour it over the set caramel, and bake in the water bath.
Chill for at least 4 hours: the custard firms, and the caramel dissolves into a sauce.
Run a thin knife round the edge, and turn it out onto a plate.

blocks.text: *Judging the wobble.* Done when the edges are set and the centre wobbles like a jelly, not a liquid, when the ramekin is nudged. It sets further as it cools. A knife in the centre comes out with a thin coat. Probe one: every part at least 71 °C (the egg-thickened row of assessment §9).

*Adapting.* A larger dish takes longer than ramekins at the same heat, because the heat has further to travel to the centre. Start checking the ramekins early, and the dish later; judge both by the wobble and log the times.
**Practice:**

items.text: ***Crème caramel* (60 min, plus 4 hours' chilling).** Caramel, custard and water bath; four ramekins and one larger dish; the wobble judged and the times logged; unmoulded.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a smooth, glossy custard with no bubbles; a clean unmoulding with a pool of caramel; an even texture right through when cut.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: No water bath, so the custard bubbles and curdles
Baking until the centre is firm, so it turns grainy and weeps
Off the heat at deep amber

blocks.text: **Safety:** caramel is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin: pour it slowly, keep a bowl of cold water nearby for your fingers, and keep children away. The custards are chilled within 2 hours, and kept at most 2 days.
**Record:** the times for the ramekins and the dish; the photos of the unmoulded custards and a cut one.

**Why it matters:** whipped cream finishes half the desserts of this course, and the difference between soft and stiff peaks decides whether it folds, fills or pipes. Over-whipped cream is a common mistake, and it can be rescued.
**You need:** 500 ml of whipping cream (*slagroom*), cold; a cold bowl; a whisk or the mixer; icing sugar and vanilla; a few spoons of extra liquid cream; *mascarpone* or *kwark* (optional).
**Explanation:**

*Whipping.* Cream of at least 30 % fat (Dutch *slagroom* is about 35 %), cold, in a cold bowl. As you whip, the fat droplets, partly crystallised, join into a network around the air bubbles (`SCI-2.M4.L1`). Warm cream has liquid fat, which can't form that network, so it won't whip. Light cooking cream (*kookroom*) has too little fat.
*The peaks.* Lift the whisk and look:

items.text: **soft:** the peak flops over; for folding into mousses and serving with cake;
**medium:** the tip bends; for filling;
**stiff:** it stands up; for piping and stabilising.

blocks.text: The last stage goes fast. With an electric whisk, switch to a hand whisk near the end, so you can stop exactly.
*Chantilly:* cream whipped with a little icing sugar and vanilla, added when it starts to thicken.

*Rescuing over-whipped cream.* When it turns grainy, fold in a few spoons of liquid cream by hand, until it is smooth again. Taken much further, it becomes butter and buttermilk, which can both be used: the butter for cooking, the buttermilk for the muffins of `BAK-2.M2.L1`.
*Stabilising* for a filling that must hold for hours: a spoon of *mascarpone*, or *kwark*, folded in.
*Keeping.* Whipped cream is kept covered in the fridge and used the same day or the next.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Peaks and a rescue (30 min).** Whip cream to soft, medium and stiff peaks, photographing each; over-whip a portion until grainy, and rescue it with liquid cream.

blocks.text: **Look for:** peaks that match the target; a smooth, glossy surface; the rescued cream smooth again.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Cream that won't hold a peak
An electric whisk left running until it turns grainy
Finish by hand; fold in liquid cream

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the photos of the three peaks and the rescue.

exercises.title: Custards and creams for a tart
exercises.description: *Crème pâtissière* used in the tart from `BAK-2.M3.X2`.

blocks.text: **Task:** make a *crème pâtissière* for the tart of `BAK-2.M3.X2`, a *crème anglaise* to *nappe*, and baked custards in ramekins and in one larger dish, with the timing adapted for the size. Cool and store everything safely, with the temperatures logged.

**You need:** 1 litre of milk; about 10 eggs; 200 g of sugar; 40 g of cornflour; vanilla; 250 ml of cream; a heavy pan; the probe; a shallow tray and film; an ice bath; ramekins and a larger dish; a roasting tin; the cooling log.
**Recipe:**

items.text: **Pastry cream:** heat 500 ml of milk with vanilla. Whisk 4 yolks, 80 g of sugar and 40 g of cornflour; temper with a third of the milk; return to the pan; whisk to the boil and boil for 1–2 minutes.
**Cool it** in the tray, film on the surface; probe and log it from 57 °C to 21 °C (within 2 hours) and to 5 °C (within 6 hours).

***Crème anglaise:*** heat 250 ml of milk; whisk 3 yolks with 40 g of sugar; temper; stir over low heat to *nappe*, probing: stop at 80–84 °C. Strain it into a bowl in the ice bath, stir until cold, and log it.

**Baked custards:** warm 250 ml of milk and the cream with vanilla; whisk gently into 3 eggs and 60 g of sugar; strain. Fill three ramekins and one larger dish. Bake in a water bath at about 150–160 °C; judge each by the wobble, probe the centre to at least 71 °C, and log both times. Chill them within 2 hours.
**Photograph** each cream on a spoon, the custards unmoulded or spooned out and cut, and the filled tart.
**Write** in two sentences how much longer the dish took, and why.

blocks.text: Keep the 7 whites for `BAK-2.M4.X3`.
**Show:**

items.text: **`TS-EGG` level 4, the custard part:** a stirred custard and a baked custard, the baked one adapted for size, to standard. With the *sabayon* and poached eggs of `SAU-2.M5.X1`, this completes the row.
**`TS-BAK` level 3, the cream element:** a smooth pastry cream that sets and holds in the tart.
**`IN-DAI` level 3, the custard part:** a stirred custard taken to *nappe* without curdling, probed. With `LEG-2.M3.X1`, the row is complete.

blocks.text: AI review scores the spoon photos: *competent* is a glossy, lump-free pastry cream and a smooth *anglaise* with a clean line; *not yet* is lumps, a grainy *anglaise*, or a missing cooling log.
**Time:** 2 h, plus chilling.

items.question: Why must *crème pâtissière* boil for a minute or two?

options.text: to gelatinise the starch fully and destroy the yolk enzyme that would thin it

items.question: Why mustn't a *crème anglaise* boil?

options.text: with no starch to protect them, the yolks curdle above about 84 °C

items.question: How do you cool a batch of pastry cream?

options.text: in the pan on the stove
spread thin in a shallow tray, film on the surface, from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours and to 5 °C within 6 hours
in a deep bowl in the fridge, still hot

items.question: Why are baked custards cooked in a water bath?

options.text: the water stays at or below 100 °C, so the custard sets gently without bubbles or curdling

items.question: Your *crème caramel* in a larger dish is still liquid in the centre when the ramekins are done. What do you do?
items.answer: Leave it in for longer, checking the wobble every 5 minutes: done when the edges are set and the centre wobbles like jelly, not liquid.
items.why: Size changes timing; judge the wobble.

items.question: A baked custard is grainy and weeping. Why?

options.text: overbaked or baked too hot, so the proteins tightened and squeezed out liquid

items.question: Cream won't whip. The most likely cause?

options.text: it is too warm, or too low in fat

items.why: The fat must be cold and plentiful.

items.question: Your whipped cream has gone grainy. Rescue it.
items.answer: Fold in a few spoons of cold liquid cream by hand until it's smooth again; don't whisk further.
items.why: Liquid cream loosens an over-whipped network.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. Its only judgment objective, reviewing your own baking, is shown in the log review rather than by scenario items; the variable items of the biscuit test were checked in `SCI-2.M1`.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** chewy or crisp, thick or thin: every biscuit comes from a few variables you can control. Changing one at a time, and seeing exactly what it does, is the method of every test you will run as a cook.

**You need:** for each batch, about 250 g of flour, 125 g of butter, 125 g of sugar (white and brown), an egg, 2 g of baking powder, a pinch of salt; two sheet pans and baking paper; a scoop or spoon and the scale, so every biscuit weighs the same; a ruler.
**Explanation:**
*The variables of a biscuit:*

rows: Chilled dough, rested overnight (less spread, deeper flavour)
Pulled while the centre is soft

blocks.text: *One variable at a time* (`RD-TEST`, `SCI-2.M1`): one control dough and one changed dough, otherwise identical. Weigh each ball of dough (for example 30 g), bake them on the same tray, at about 180 °C, and taste them blind. Measure the spread with a ruler.
*Dutch biscuits* to try the framework on:

items.text: ***boterkoekjes*:** rich, short butter biscuits;
***speculaas*** in winter: spiced, thin and crisp;
***kletskoppen*:** very thin and crisp, from a high-sugar, high-butter dough that spreads.

blocks.text: *Reading the results.* Spread comes from fat melting before the structure sets, and from sugar dissolving; chew comes from moisture held by brown sugar and egg yolk, and from gluten. If the result surprised you, the table usually shows why.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A chewy and a crisp biscuit (50 min).** The same base formula changed in sugar and fat: brown sugar and melted butter for one, white sugar and creamed butter for the other. Photograph them side by side.
**The rested dough (50 min, the next day).** The same dough baked straight, and after a night in the fridge; the spread measured with a ruler.

blocks.text: **Look for:** spread and texture that follow the variable as predicted; biscuits of equal size on one tray.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Pull them while the centre is soft

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific; the trays come out with gloves.
**Record:** the photos, the spread measurements and the predictions.

**Why it matters:** after seven weeks the baking log holds a dozen or more bakes. Read together, they show what single bakes can't: an oven that always runs hot, a habit of underbaking, or an eye that is kinder to itself than the tasters are.
**You need:** the baking log, with its photos and bands; the AI review and taster bands; the journal.
**Explanation:**
*Reviewing a stage of baking.* Read the log for patterns:

items.text: **recurring faults:** an oven that runs hot, dry cakes, pale bases;
**the variables that changed them:** what you did differently in the bakes that worked;
**agreement:** where your own band agreed with the AI review and the tasters, and where it didn't (`JD-REFL`).

blocks.text: *Calibrating your eye.* Agreement within one band in at least four of five entries shows that your eye is calibrated. Read the disagreements for a direction: do you always rate yourself higher, or lower? Do you disagree on one kind of bake (the crumb of cakes, the colour of pastry)? A direction tells you what to look at harder next time.
*Targets.* Write two or three, as practice for `BRD-2` and `PST-3`. A target is specific and checkable:

items.text: "blind bake 5 minutes longer, until the base is golden";
"weigh the eggs";
"check the thermometer before every bake".

blocks.text: Targets like "be more careful" can't be checked, so they don't change anything.

*The format.* A page: a table of the five chosen entries (the bake, your band, the AI or taster band, the difference), then the patterns in a few sentences, each citing an entry and its photo, then the targets.
**Practice:** theory only (1.5 h): read the baking log, mark the agreements and disagreements, and write the review and the targets.
**Look for:** a review that cites entries and photos, finds a pattern, and sets specific targets.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: The same blind spot next stage

blocks.text: **Safety:** none specific.
**Record:** the review page and the targets, in the journal (in `BAK-2.M6.X1`).

exercises.title: The biscuit test, and the log review
exercises.description: The biscuit variable test with household tasters.

blocks.text: **Task:** test one biscuit variable with household tasters, and review the course's baking log against the AI review and the tasters. Choose one variable from the table of `BAK-2.M6.L1`, and write the prediction. The household tastes blind on the form. For the log review, take five entries from the course: one each from `BAK-2.M2` to `BAK-2.M5`, and the biscuits.

**You need:** a biscuit formula twice: about 250 g of flour, 125 g of butter, 125 g of sugar and an egg per batch, with 2 g of baking powder and a pinch of salt; two sheet pans; the scale; a ruler; the comparison template; the tasting forms; the baking log.
**Framework:** the test and the review.

rows: The base formula, creamed, in 30 g balls
One change from the table; everything else identical
Spread, texture and taste, written on the template
Control and variable on one tray, at about 180 °C, the same time
The spread of five biscuits each, with a ruler
Five entries; your band against the AI or taster band; patterns; two or three targets

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Write the prediction.
Bake the control and the variable on one tray.
Measure the spread.
Taste blind.
Write the conclusion.
Choose the five log entries, set the bands side by side, and write the review and the targets.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`RD-TEST` level 2:** a comparison with one variable changed, recorded on the template, with the blind tasting.

**`JD-REFL` level 3:** five entries where your band agrees with the AI or the tasters within one band in at least four, with the review and the targets. The edge log of `KNF-2.M3.X1` is a first set of five.

blocks.text: AI review scores the side-by-side photo: *competent* is biscuits of equal size with a visible difference that matches the variable; *not yet* is unequal sizes, or two variables changed.
**Time:** 2 h.
